title: Peter Martyr's own words against habitual grace that makes pleasing
source_text: X. Hanc autem esse Doctorum illorum sententiam patet ex ipsorum verbis. Sic enim Petrus Martyr in locis communibus Classe tertia loco secundo numero octavo de gratia infusa Scholasticorum loquens, Non est, inquit, parvus error quod volunt nos hoc habitu, seu creatura reddi gratos Deo. Necessarium enim est, cum ille nos hujusmodi dono affecerit, eum nos amasse prius. Amor enim Dei praecedit omnia ejus dona: Et numero decimo tertio. Nec minus errant, inquit, qui garriunt in scholis, aliam esse gratiam gratis datam, aliam gratum facientem. Omnem enim gratiam oportet gratis dari. Nam alioqui, ut Paulus ait, non esset gratia. Cumque per gratiam gratum facientem intelligant habitum, ut supra docuimus, male statuunt homines per ejusmodi dona apud Deum gratos effici. Nam apud eum per solam ejus misericordiam, & propter Christum recipimur in gratiam.
pass_a_gloss: X. But that this is the opinion of those Doctors is plain from their own words. For thus Peter Martyr in the commonplaces Class three place two number eight speaking of the infused grace of the Scholastics, It is no small error, he says, that they will that we are rendered pleasing to God by this habit, or creature. For it is necessary, when he has affected us with a gift of this kind, that he loved us before. For the love of God precedes all his gifts: And at number thirteen. Nor do they err less, he says, who prate in the schools, that grace freely given is one, grace making pleasing another. For all grace must be given freely. For otherwise, as Paul says, it would not be grace. And since by grace making pleasing they understand a habit, as we taught above, men wrongly determine that by gifts of this kind they are made pleasing before God. For with him by his mercy alone, and for Christ's sake we are received into favour.
pass_b_english: Thesis X. That this is what those doctors hold is clear from their own words. Peter Martyr, in his Commonplaces (class 3, locus 2, paragraph 8), speaking of the scholastics' infused grace, writes: It is no small error that they want us to be made pleasing to God by this habit or created thing. When he has endowed us with such a gift, he must have loved us first, for God's love comes before all his gifts.

And in paragraph 13 he says: Those who chatter in the schools that grace freely given is one thing and grace that makes pleasing another are just as wrong. All grace has to be given freely, for otherwise, as Paul says, it would not be grace. And since by grace that makes pleasing they mean a habit, as we showed above, they are wrong to lay down that people become pleasing to God through such gifts. With him we are received into favour by his mercy alone and for Christ's sake.

choices.why: The scholastic pair (Aquinas, Summa theologiae I-II q. 111 a. 1): gifts given for the good of others versus the grace that makes its bearer pleasing to God. Kept literal because the Reformed objections turn on the very words.
